changelog: Delete C4: it largely restates C3 (clausal material supplying predicate/argument/scope) and encourages attention to noun-phrase internal boundaries; removing this redundant rule reduces rule competition that can push cuts into multiword names/NPs (the critique and history show clausal-attachment rules can force cuts inside NPs and named entities).
findings: The prompt allows cuts inside multiword proper names or titles, treating internal boundaries as acceptable splits and so fragmenting named entities.
The prompt cuts immediately after fronted temporal/adverbial phrases, detaching them from their governing verb and producing incoherent or misleading early pieces.

When forced to choose between two imperfect internal cuts, the prompt prefers cuts that break verb–object adjacency; instead it should prefer cuts that avoid separating a verb from its core object/complement.

diagnosis.why: Removing C4 removed a protection against cutting at noun-phrase / name-internal boundaries, so the scorer began placing earlier cuts inside multiword NPs/named entities (examples: 'John ‖ Nixon', 'Cirque ‖ du Soleil', 'We ‖ will ‖ never...'). That change raised agreement at rank‑1 but worsened ranks 2–3 (rank_depth: +0.124 at depth1, −0.216/−0.098 at depths2–3), produced mixed counts (n_better 2287 vs n_worse 1926), and caused a measurable drop in the mid‑length bin (≤10: −0.0044).
diagnosis.lesson: If you remove a rule that overlaps clausal-attachment checks, keep an explicit constraint (or reweighting) that prevents cuts inside multiword names/NP-internal boundaries so top choice gains don’t come at the expense of deeper-ranked cuts used by shorter-latency budgets.
